To assess transistor performance with A-TiO2 gate oxide, we measured 100 p- and 100 n-type devices across the wafer, randomly sampled from five representative regions (Supplementary Fig. 11), where the majority of devices have consistent electrical characteristics across the wafer. Devices were qualified by excluding those with abnormal Vth shifts, Ion/Ioff outside 106–5 × 107, or failed electrical characteristics. Figure 2e shows representative transfer characteristics (Ids – Vgs) of 80 qualified long-channel 1L-MoS2 FETs integrated with a 5.8-nm-thick A-TiO2 dielectric (EOT ≈ 0.88 nm; W/L = 2 μm/3 μm). The average subthreshold swing across the array is 68 mV dec–1, with the best device achieving 61 mV dec–1. Similarly, 84 qualified bilayer WSe2 (2L-WSe2) FETs (W/L = 2 μm/2 μm) with A-TiO2 dielectric show excellent performance (Fig. 2f), delivering average and minimum subthreshold swing values of 79 mV dec–1 and 65 mV dec–1, respectively. The subthreshold swing values as a function of Ids for selected 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 and 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 devices are presented in Supplementary Fig. 13. Statistical distributions of Ion/Ioff, subthreshold swing and Vth for the working p- and n-type transistors are summarized in Supplementary Fig. 12, with most n- and p-FETs (>98%) exhibiting over seven orders of magnitude in Ion/Ioff ratios, low gate leakage and minimal variation in Vth. Supplementary Fig. 14a and 14b further present representative transfer characteristics of 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs integrated with thicker A-TiO2 gate dielectrics (18.2 nm; EOT ≈ 1.5 nm). Supplementary Fig. 14c–f show the corresponding gate leakage currents for 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs with 18.2-nm and 5.8 nm A-TiO2 gate dielectrics, supporting that strong electrostatic control is maintained without increased leakage even under aggressive EOT scaling. Extended Data Fig. 3a compares the subthreshold swing versus EOT across various technologies using CVD-grown 2D channels. Extended Data Fig. 3b further compares Jleak at an applied gate voltage of 1 V for various gate-stack technologies with EOT or CET ≤ 1 nm. The A-TiO2 gate stack demonstrates low Jleak with sub-1-nm EOT, remaining well below the low-power limit (1.5 × 10−2 A cm−2). Recent studies have highlighted the trade-off between leakage-current suppression and electrostatic scaling in vdW-integrated 2D transistor interfaces31, and readers are referred to these works for broader discussions on EOT benchmarking and scaling considerations.

We further fabricated short-channel bottom-gated 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs with channel lengths of about 50 nm to evaluate gate controllability at scaled dimensions. Even at this reduced channel length, both 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 and 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 devices exhibit near-ideal subthreshold swing (around 72 mV dec–1) and a high Ion/Ioff ratio (>108) without an increase in off-state current (Fig. 2g,h). The short-channel devices also have high Ion at Vds = 0.6 V. For the 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 configuration, Ion reaches 227 μA μm–1 at Vov = 0.6 V and 167 μA μm–1 at Vov = 0.4 V. Similarly, the 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 device demonstrates Ion values of 136 μA μm–1 (Vov = –0.6 V) and 86 μA μm–1 (Vov = –0.4 V) at a drain bias of –0.6 V, where Vov = Vgs − Vth denotes the gate-overdrive voltage. The corresponding output characteristics are shown in Fig. 2i. These results can be attributed to the superior gate-to-channel electrostatic control enabled by the A-TiO2 high-κ gate stack (Extended Data Fig. 4). Figure 2j benchmarks the subthreshold swing versus channel length (Lch) for reported short-channel 2D FETs using different dielectric technologies, highlighting that the subthreshold swing values achieved with A-TiO2 gate dielectric are among the lowest reported for CVD-grown MoS2 and WSe2 devices with similar structures. Supplementary Table 1 benchmarks devices using amorphous or single-crystal gate dielectrics with CVD-grown 2D TMD channel materials. The proposed A-TiO2 integration achieves a sub-1-nm EOT, a subthreshold swing of below 65 mV dec–1 and a high Ion, metrics which align with the requirements for low-power, high-performance logic applications.

Hysteresis in the transistor transfer characteristics is a critical metric of operational stability. Here we systematically compare 2D transistors integrated with single-crystalline A-TiO2 to those using amorphous HfO2 and Al2O3 gate dielectrics deposited by the ALD approach (Methods). Extended Data Fig. 5 displays the Ids – Vgs characteristics for different types of dielectrics under forward and reverse gate-voltage sweeps. The hysteresis width (ΔVH) of 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FETs reaches an exceptionally small value of around 1.5 mV at the sweeping frequency (f) of 0.028 Hz (f = 1/tsw, where tsw represents the total forward and backward sweeping time). The cyclostationary behavior of the 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FET is further detailed in Supplementary Fig. 15. The minimal variation observed between the initial and 100th measurement cycles supports the robustness of the gate stack and ensures that our hysteresis characterization is reliable for future device benchmarking32. For a fair comparison, ΔVH is normalized by EOT33,34. Figure 3a summarizes the statistical distribution of normalized ΔVH extracted from devices employing different dielectrics (Supplementary Fig. 16), where A-TiO2 has the smallest hysteresis value among all the tested devices. Supplementary Fig. 17 further shows normalized ΔVH as a function of sweep frequency for a representative 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FET measured under different gate sweeping ranges. The resulting hysteresis remains minimal across all measurement conditions, in sharp contrast to MoS2 transistors with conventional SiO2, Al2O3 or HfO2 gate dielectrics, which display pronounced hysteresis, particularly at low sweeping frequencies, due to slow charge trapping in oxide defect states35. Figure 3b benchmarks the normalized ΔVH of 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FETs against literature values reported for a range of dielectric technologies. Notably, our unencapsulated devices achieve a normalized ΔVH of 0.5 mV nm–1, which not only outperforms those of unencapsulated 2D transistors but also demonstrates superior stability compared with channel-encapsulated devices. Furthermore, bias-temperature instability (BTI) measurements reinforce the stability of the 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 interface (Methods), revealing small threshold voltage shift (ΔVth) under both positive (ΔVth = 40 mV) and negative (ΔVth = 50 mV) gate bias stress (Supplementary Fig. 18). These results indicate the scarcity of border traps within the single-crystalline gate dielectric and a clean dielectric/2D semiconductor interface, even when integrated using conventional wet transfer technologies. Although the BTI of these 2D FETs currently exceeds that of established silicon technology3, further optimization of the interface and dielectric quality remains a clear path toward industrial parity.

Open and solid symbols denote amorphous and crystalline gate dielectrics, respectively. All benchmark values were extracted for 2 V < ΔVgs < 3.5 V and tsw ≤ 100 s. c, Typical cross-sectional STM topography image of the Au/TiO2 interface. Scale bar, 10 nm. d, Atomic-scale evolution of electronic properties of the subsurface of A-TiO2 and HfO2. e, Arrhenius plot of I-DLTS results extracted from 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 and 1L-MoS2/HfO2 devices, revealing two distinct trap states. The table in the inset lists the activation energy (Ec – Et) and the capture cross section (σn) of two trap states, obtained from the slope and intercept of the two Arrhenius curves. f, Transfer characteristics of 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 (green) and 2L-WSe2/HfO2 (purple) p-FETs. Both devices share identical channel dimensions (Lch = 2 μm, Wch = 2 μm), highlighting the impact of dielectric choice on FET devices.

The record-low hysteresis can be attributed to the clean channel–dielectric interface and crystalline dielectric with low concentration of traps, which together drastically suppress charge trapping to enable low hysteresis. The estimated interface trap density (Dit) is determined as approximately 5.74 × 1011 cm−2 eV−1, substantially lower than the values typically reported for devices incorporating CVD-grown MoS2 channels (Supplementary Table 2), although CVD-synthesized MoS2 inevitably contains point defects (1011–1012 cm–2) due to thermodynamic and growth chemistry constraints36. To understand the origin of hysteresis, we perform cross-sectional scanning tunneling microscope/spectroscopy (XSTM/S) measurements to directly probe the in-gap states in dielectric oxides (Supplementary Note 1). A representative XSTM topography of the metal–dielectric interface is shown in Fig. 3c, whereas spatially resolved XSTM-STS measurements acquired at sub-0.5 nm intervals from the interface into the dielectric are presented in Fig. 3d. Amorphous HfO2 has pronounced in-gap states near the band edges, particularly close to the interface, indicating a high density of charge-trapping centres. By contrast, no discernible in-gap states are detected in A-TiO2, supporting its intrinsically low trap density.

Moreover, current-mode deep-level transient spectroscopy (I-DLTS) reveals distinct trap characteristics at 1L-MoS2/dielectric interfaces (Fig. 3e). 1L-MoS2/HfO2 has a shallow trap (0.221 eV below Ec) with a large capture cross-section (σn = 1.40 × 10−13 cm2). Conversely, 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 shows a deeper trap at 0.293 eV below Ec with a capture cross-section that is three orders of magnitude smaller (σn = 6.40 × 10−17 cm2), substantially suppressing trapping (Supplementary Note 2). The close agreement between XSTM-STS and I-DLTS measurements indicates that shallow, Coulomb-attractive traps dominate the 1L-MoS2/HfO2 interface, whereas deeper, near-neutral traps in A-TiO2   exhibit substantially lower trapping probability. The influence of dielectric quality is further illustrated in Fig. 3f, which compares the transfer characteristics of WSe2 p-FETs fabricated with A-TiO2 and amorphous HfO2 gate dielectrics. The A-TiO2-gated device has clean unipolar p-type behaviour across the entire gate sweep; however, the HfO2-gated device shows pronounced bipolar transport, incompatible with robust CMOS operation. This contrast indicates that the bipolar response is linked to defect-induced Fermi-level modulation associated with in-gap states in the amorphous dielectric (Supplementary Note 3). These findings underscore the critical importance of using high-quality dielectrics with low-trap density to achieve stable, unipolar p-type operation in WSe2 FETs.

The stable and high-performance A-TiO2-gated 2D FETs motivate us to further demonstrate their scalable vertical integration into complementary field-effect transistors (CFETs) (Fig. 4a). Fabrication begins with MoS2 n-FET arrays, using buried gold electrodes as source and drain contacts and single-crystalline A-TiO2 as the top-gate dielectric. A vertical CMOS architecture is then constructed by stacking 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 p-FET arrays directly above the n-type tier, sharing a common Pt gate electrode. After vertically interconnecting the drain electrodes of n- and p-FETs through the via-metal, where the output voltage (Vout) is measured, the CFET inverters are realized (the schematic structure is shown in Fig. 4b; refer to Extended Data Fig. 6 for detailed fabrication steps). Figure 4c shows the cross-sectional HRTEM images acquired at the channel region of a representative CFET inverter, revealing uniformly flat layers with atomically sharp vdW interfaces between the 2D semiconductors and the A-TiO2 gate dielectrics. An overview cross-sectional HRTEM image of the complete CFET stack, illustrating the vertical alignment of the top p-FET and bottom n-FET tiers, is provided in Extended Data Fig. 7.

The transfer curves of the bottom n-FETs and top p-FETs (Lch = 1 μm) measured from 16 CFETs are shown in Fig. 4d, exhibiting nearly symmetric behavior and limited device-to-device variation. Note that the voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) curves shown for the CFET inverters exclude abnormal devices (Supplementary Note 4). The yield of the CFET inverters is approximately 50% (25 functional devices out of 50 fabricated devices) and requires further engineering improvement. The standard deviations of normalized Ion are 21.8% for the n-FETs and 23.9% for the p-FETs. The average Vth is 0.9 V for the n-FETs and −1.1 V for the p-FETs, confirming enhancement-mode operation for both device types, which is essential for low-power logic applications. Both n- and p-FETs have steep subthreshold slopes, indicating high transconductance ( gm, defined as the change in drain current with respect to gate voltage, ∆Ids/∆Vgs) and transconductance efficiency (gm/Ids), which are essential for achieving large voltage gain in CFET inverters. Consistently, both device types maintain Ion/Ioff ratios exceeding 107 over a range of Vds while preserving a minimum subthreshold swing of about 75 mV dec–1 (Supplementary Fig. 19), enabling efficient inverter operation at reduced supply voltage (Vdd) with low power consumption. Figure 4e displays representative VTCs of the CFET inverters, demonstrating excellent full-rail logic swing across a range of Vdd from 0.1 V to 1 V. The voltage gain increases progressively with Vdd, from 12 V/V at 0.25 V to a peak value of 89 V/V at 1 V. Remarkably, even at the minimum Vdd of 0.1 V, the inverter maintains a gain value exceeding the minimum threshold (1 V/V) for functional logic operation37, highlighting the potential of this CFET architecture for ultra-low-voltage, energy-efficient circuits. Supplementary Fig. 20 summarizes the voltage gain, static power consumption (Pstatic) and estimated noise margins (NML, low-level noise margin; NMH, high-level noise margin) as functions of Vdd, extracted from 16 individual CFET inverters. Owing to the crystalline nature of the high-κ dielectric and well-matched characteristics of n/p-FETs, the CFET inverters had ultralow gate and channel leakage currents during operation, resulting in exceptionally low Pstatic. At Vdd = 0.25 V, Pstatic is measured to be 38 fW, and even at Vdd = 1 V it remains as low as 1 pW. As summarized in Fig. 4f, the achieved Pstatic is the lowest reported among 2D material-based CMOS inverters, while simultaneously maintaining high gain.

Figure 4g compares the voltage gain values versus switch point (VM/Vdd), where VM denotes the input voltage at which Vout equals Vin. A switching point near 0.5 is critical for maximizing noise margins and ensuring symmetric logic operation. The CFET inverters demonstrated here not only achieve high voltage gains but also maintain VM/Vdd values close to the ideal 0.5. To further evaluate the noise tolerance of our CFET inverters, we estimated the noise margin (NM% = NML% + NMH%) values from the VTCs for 16 individual devices. The average NM% values are 67.5%, 82.5%, 87.5% and 89.2% at Vdd values of 0.25 V, 0.5 V, 0.75 V and 1 V, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 20), exceeding previously reported CFET implementations (Extended Data Table 1).

Beyond inverter operation, logic gate networks, including NAND and NOR gates, were implemented using CFET-based pull-up and pull-down configurations comprising two p-FETs and two n-FETs (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 21). Both logic gates operate reliably at a low Vdd of 0.5 V, demonstrating the feasibility of CFET-based logic beyond single-inverter circuits. The thermal stability of A-TiO2-integrated CFETs was evaluated at both material and device levels (Supplementary Note 5). The results support that the A-TiO2 dielectric and its interfaces with TMD channels retain electrical and crystallographic integrity under  back-end-of-line (BEOL) thermal conditions (up to 400 °C). However, extended high-temperature exposure beyond conventional limits causes noticeable device degradation.

Furthermore, the electrical performance of short-channel CFET inverters with about 50 nm channel lengths in both the bottom- and top-tier FETs was also evaluated (Extended Data Fig. 8a). The transfer characteristics of the p-FET and n-FET show well-matched threshold voltages and on-currents (Extended Data Fig. 8b). This electrical symmetry enables a high inverter voltage gain (gain = 97 V/V at Vdd = 1 V). The improvement is attributed to the higher switching current enabled by the short channels, as illustrated in the VTC and corresponding gain curve in Extended Data Fig. 8c,d. As expected, the static power consumption of these short-channel devices is higher than that of long-channel (Lch = 1 μm) CFETs, as a result of increased short-circuit current and Ioff during switching (Extended Data Fig. 8e). Further work on integrating Vth-tuning techniques is needed to achieve the critical balance of high gain and low power consumption in our CFET technology. Furthermore, we estimate dynamic power (Pdyn) (Supplementary Note 6), where the analysis indicates that the scaled CFET achieves a 39% reduction in dynamic power (Pdyn ≈ 230.3 nW, Vdd = 0.5 V), compared with the long-channel counterpart (Pdyn ≈ 378.3 nW, Vdd = 0.5 V). This improvement arises from reduced intrinsic and Miller capacitances associated with the scaled geometry, which outweighs the additional parasitic coupling introduced by the vertical stacking38,39.

In summary, this work demonstrates a 3-inch freestanding A-TiO2 membrane as a gate dielectric that delivers exceptional thickness uniformity and favourable dielectric metrics. The atomically clean interface formed between A-TiO2 and 2D materials enables low subthreshold swing, record-low hysteresis and well-balanced enhancement-mode operation for both n- and p-type transistors. Building on this gate-stack platform, vertically stacked CFET inverter arrays have high voltage gain, wide noise margins and ultralow static power consumption. Density functional theory (DFT) combined with NEGF (NEGF-DFT) simulations further project that the proposed 2D CFET architecture can be scaled to the 1-nm node while sustaining stable operation (Supplementary Note 7). Together, these results establish wafer-scale single-crystal high-κ dielectrics integrated with 2D semiconductors as viable and promising platforms for energy-efficient logic technologies, positioning them as compelling candidates for the post-silicon electronics roadmap.

The AlO2-terminated surface of single-crystalline 3-inch LaAlO3 (001) substrates was prepared by wet etching of LaAlO3 (001) for 30 s with dilute HCl (pH ≈ 4.5), followed by 1,000 °C annealing in a pure oxygen atmosphere. The atomically sharp step and terraces of substrates were examined by AFM. The SrTiO3, Sr3Al2O6 and A-TiO2 films were grown by pulsed laser deposition using a 248-nm krypton fluoride excimer laser with a laser fluence of 48 mJ cm–2. A laser-scanning system capable of depositing films on wafers up to 4-inch in diameter was used, in which a linear translation stage, rather than a galvanometer, was used to scan the laser beam across a rotating target. This configuration eliminates optical distortions and maintains consistent ablation conditions, thereby ensuring uniform film growth. The SrTiO3 buffer layer and water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 layers were deposited at 850 °C with an oxygen partial pressure (\({p}_{{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\)) of 1 × 10−6 torr. The in situ RHEED patterns indicated the highly crystalline nature for the as-grown A-TiO2 layer, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 1a). The epitaxial growth of the A-TiO2 layer on the Sr3Al2O6 thin film was then conducted at 800 °C and \({p}_{{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\) = 1 × 10−4 torr. On the completion of film deposition, the sample was cooled down to room temperature under \({p}_{{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\) = 1 × 10−1 torr to prevent non-stoichiometry in A-TiO2 film.

The 1L-MoS2 film was synthesized via a CVD method on C/M sapphire substrates (supplied by Crystal-wise Technology), which had undergone surface reconstruction. Molybdenum trioxide (MoO3, 99.5%) and sulfur (S, 99.5%) powders (both from Sigma-Aldrich) were positioned in separate zones of a quartz tube furnace. A heating belt regulated the sulfur evaporation at 160–180 °C, whereas the substrate and MoO3 were heated to 700 °C. An argon gas flow facilitated the transport of vapourized precursors. The growth process lasted 15 min, after which the system was allowed to cool naturally to room temperature. The 2L-WSe2 film was provided by Nexstrom, where the samples were grown by CVD methods. The transfer procedures of 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 follow the common polymethyl-methacrylate-assisted wet transfer method.

X-ray diffraction measurements were conducted using a Rigaku SmartLab thin-film XRD system with a rotating copper anode X-ray source. The dislocation density (\(\rho \)) is evaluated using the Vannas (Halliwell–Hirsch) model:

where \(\beta \) is the FWHM in radians and \(b\) is the Burgers vector. The surface morphologies were examined by AFM (Bruker Dimension Icon SPM). The film thickness uniformity was measured by an ellipsometer (J.A. Woollam RC2). Raman and Photoluminescence spectra of MoS2 and WSe2 were collected in a confocal Raman microscopy system (WITec alpha 300 R) with a 532-nm laser. The cross-sectional STM measurement was conducted under ultrahigh vacuum (5 × 10−11 torr) at room temperature. Plan-view dark-field TEM image and SAED pattern of A-TiO2 membrane were captured using a Thermo Scientific Talos F200X STEM at 200 kV from a top-view sample suspended on a holey carbon grid. Cross-section lamellas for LaAlO3//SrTiO3//Sr3Al2O6//A-TiO2 heterostructure, single FET and CFET devices were prepared with a focused-ion-beam system (Thermo Scientific Helios 5 CX). Cross-section STEM images and EDS mapping were conducted by the same STEM system at 200 kV. The surface topography and structure of CFET logic gates were examined by SEM (Zeiss Sigma 300 VP).

For MIM capacitors, the A-TiO2 membranes were transferred onto Au-coated Si substrates; subsequently, 10 nm Ti and 80 nm Au electrodes were fabricated through the shadow mask by electron-beam evaporation. For ALD-grown amorphous dielectric oxides, we used trimethylaluminum and water as the precursors for Al2O3 deposition, whereas tetrakis (dimethylamido) hafnium and water served as the precursors for HfO2, with the growth temperature of 150 °C. For FET fabrication (Supplementary Fig. 8), the A-TiO2 membranes and 1L-MoS2/2L-WSe2 layers were sequentially transferred onto a Ti/Pt (1 nm/8 nm) local back-gate array. The channel area was defined using electron-beam lithography followed by O2 reactive-ion etching (10 mTorr, 100 W). After patterning the source/drain regions using electron-beam lithography, Sb/Au (20 nm/40 nm) and Pt/Au (5 nm/15 nm) contacts were deposited to form n-type 1L-MoS2 and p-type 2L-WSe2 FETs, respectively. The metals were deposited using thermal and e-beam evaporation, and the chamber pressure was maintained at around 10−8 Torr throughout the metal deposition process. For CFET devices (Extended Data Fig. 6), a 12-nm Au layer was first deposited on the substrate to serve as the bottom contact for the n-FET. A 1L-MoS2 film was transferred and patterned, followed by the transfer of an A-TiO2 membrane as the gate dielectric. A 10-nm Pt mid-gate was then defined on A-TiO2 to serve as the shared gate for both bottom n-FET and top p-FET. The top device was then completed by sequential transfer of a second A-TiO2 membrane and a 2L-WSe2 film, which was intentionally adopted to improve device-to-device uniformity and process tolerance during multilayer CFET fabrication, supported by independent statistical comparison of 1L-WSe2 and 2L-WSe2 devices (Supplementary Note 8). To remove surface polymer residue, a mild O2 plasma treatment (15 W, 20 s) and hot-acetone vapour (80 °C, 30 min) were applied after transferring the A-TiO2 and 2D material layers, respectively. After electron-beam lithography alignment of the active regions, 5 nm Pt/20 nm Au were deposited to form the p-FET contacts. Finally, the CFET inverter was formed by interconnecting the two pads respectively from n- and p-FETs through a via opening defined by O2/SF6 inductively coupled plasma etching, followed by Au metallization. The same via process was used for NAND and NOR logic demonstrations.

Electrical characterization of the devices was performed using a Keysight B1500A semiconductor parameter analyser mounted in a closed-cycle cryogenic probe station (at a base pressure of about 10−6 Torr). Capacitance measurements were conducted with the Keysight E5288A C-V Measurement System integrated into the B1500A platform. All devices were measured under vacuum conditions within a probe station featuring a shielded enclosure to reduce electromagnetic interference. where \({C}_{\mathrm{ox}}\) is the gate dielectric capacitance obtained from MIM capacitance measurements (Extended Data Fig. 2), \(q\) is the elementary charge, \({k}_{{\rm{B}}}\) is the Boltzmann constant and \(T\) is the absolute temperature. Pstatic is calculated as \({{V}}_{{\rm{dd}}}\times ({I}_{{{\rm{Static}}}_{{\rm{low}}}}+{I}_{{{\rm{Static}}}_{{\rm{high}}}})/2\) in the static regime (Vin = 0 V or Vin = Vdd).

Bias-temperature instability measurements were performed at room temperature by applying gate biases of –1 V and +2 V, respectively, for 1,000 s. After removal of the stress bias, Vth recovery was monitored through transfer measurements at Vds = 1 V. The same extraction criterion was used throughout, and the Vth shift was calculated relative to the initial value as ΔVth = Vth,t – Vth,0.

The transport properties of the 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs were investigated using DFT combined with the NEGF formalism, as implemented in the QuantumATK package60. Here, \({V}_{\mathrm{gs}}\) and \({V}_{\mathrm{dd}}\) were set to be 0.6 V. All calculations were performed using linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO) basis set with high accuracy and PseudoDojo pseudopotential61. The exchange-correlation functional was treated at the GGA-PBE level. For the MoS2 DG-FET, a 15 × 1 × 173 Monkhorst–Pack k-point grid is used. For the 2L-WSe2 DG-FET, a 33 × 1 × 165 grid is adopted and vdW-D3 correction is used for vdW interaction62. The gate length of both devices is set to 10 nm. Two gate dielectrics are examined for electrostatic control: SiO2 with a permittivity of 3.9 and thickness of 0.9 nm, and TiO2 with a high-κ value of 25 and thickness of 5.8 nm. The atomic compensation-charge method is used to control the doping distribution in the source and drain extensions.

#1358. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

"I think sometimes we have to be more brave under pressure." Captain Bruno Fernandes gives his immediate reaction to Manchester United's heavy 4-1 defeat to Como 🗣️ 🎙️ @LiamMacdevitt 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/8bzmLGkRAX

There may be some truth in that, but Carrick’s response felt the most accurate assessment of the lot and will certainly chime with supporters who have long questioned how and why so many United sides, regardless of the manager, reach a point where running, intensity and urgency seem optional. “Whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win,” Carrick said.

Carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. He even described Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds as a “fresh start”. But Como blew the lid off any pretence of that being the case. Even by the standards of this season to date, though, what unfolded here in the rain in Lombardy was shocking to witness.

Como, inspired by the outstanding Nico Paz, were every bit as good as United – who have won just two of 11 games this season – were a pitiful mess.

Having conceded after just 47 seconds to Atlético Madrid last week, United were behind after only 118 seconds this time. That in itself told you a lot about these players and this team and it set the tone for what was to follow: a masterclass in incompetence and indifference. There have only been four worse results in United’s European history, although you will struggle to find a poorer performance than this.

Nico Paz scores a stunner to get Como ahead against Manchester United within 2 minutes! 😱 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/ikH9MVg6cB

You looked at Como and it was clear every player knew their job and role and went about it with relish. There were patterns of play, they ran, there was intensity and movement and they were quicker to everything.

Paz scored the first and third goals and set up a wondrous second for Tasos Douvikas that showcased Como’s talent at the same time as underlining United’s myriad fault lines. Paz was just unplayable for much of an evening when United never got close to getting to grips with the young Argentine, whose big physique belies a bewitching ability on the ball. Jacobo Ramón completed the rout before Joshua Zirkzee scored the most hollow of goals for United late on.

Como extend their lead to 2-0 against Manchester United early in the second half! Anastasios Douvikas gets the goal 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/2O9qRG75tG

United, by contrast, were a sorry collection of strangers. It was impossible to discern a game plan. United were sent out in a strange 4-2-4, with Fernandes and Youri Tielemans operating as almost double false nines. Glenn Hoddle said on TNT Sports that it was like United were “playing in chains”.

Neither looked sure of what they were supposed to be doing. There was just a giant hole where the attack should have been. Everything about them was slow, leaden. The confusion was contagious. Everywhere you looked there were players second-guessing themselves, uncertain of their role and position and habitually a yard or two or three off the pace. But was there any excuse for not running, for so little effort?

The space Paz was afforded to curl in a fine finish less than two minutes in was alarming in the extreme. Carrick brought on Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo for the lamentable Mateus Cunha and Andrey Santos at half-time, but United just got worse.

There was not so much as a snip at the heels of the same player when Paz ghosted in from the right flank, running 30 yards deep into the penalty area before again finishing coolly for the third. Ramón had a free header for the fourth.

Nico Paz capitalises on a mistake from Carlos Baleba to extend Como's lead against Manchester United to 3-0 😱 He's been involved in each goal 👏 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/D7kD8PGtcY

As for that second shortly after the restart? First the impressive Lucas Da Cunha rolled Baleba too easily. Noussair Mazraoui got sucked in trying to mark Martin Baturina in the middle, but got nowhere close as the Como winger played a lovely first-time pass in behind for Paz, who had run off the back of Mason Mount. Douvikas had positioned himself on Matthijs de Ligt’s blind side and the defender, making his first appearance for 11 months, had no idea where the Greece striker was before he darted across the front of him to receive Paz’s pass and dink the ball over Senne Lammens.

For Como, who were playing in Italy’s third tier five years ago, this was one of the greatest nights in their history. For United, it was one of the worst. Carrick may pay a heavy price for it, but there are far greater problems than the manager at this football club.

Paz has inherited Messi’s famous No 10 Argentina shirt, and while no current player measures up to the legendary forward, the country’s latest hero is making as a good a fist of it as any.

What of United and Carrick? Time will tell how damaging this defeat is, but they were utterly dreadful barring a four-minute spell at the start of the second half and some late invention from Amad. You simply cannot influence matches with such fleeting quality, especially at this level.

Into the final minute of time added on. Amad tiptoes past three Como players but cannot do it all by himself and the hosts clear their lines eventually.

Como 4 Manchester United 1 (Zirkzee) United get one back. Amad swings in a threatening ball over the top, which Zirkzee finishes tidily after taking a deft first touch. There is a check for offside but the goal stands.

Amad twists and turns on the by-line before thrashing a cross that ricochets off Kempf and behind for a corner. But Como clear their lines with a minimum of fuss.

Lacey goes into the book for a poor challenge straight off the bat.

Lacey gets a handful of minutes, coming on for Mbeumo.

Amad, in fairness, has at least try to make things happen. He wins a free-kick 20 yards out after contact from Kempf and the winger steps up to take the set-piece himself, but can only direct his effort straight at Butez.

Men against boys stuff here. United are playing to whatever tune Como decide now, chasing shadows, and it really isn’t a good look for Carrick, who was already under mounting pressure coming into this encounter.

De Ligt’s evening is over as 19-year-old Amass enters the field of play.

Como make a triple change as Perrone, Paz and Couto make way for Dossena, Ricci and Liberali. Paz in particular receives a rapturous ovation when his name is read out by the stadium announcer.

Paz tries to curl the ball from the right of the box as Como sweep the ball from left to right at pace, but it’s too close to Lammens and the Belgian gathers.

Como 4 Manchester United 0 (Ramon) Perhaps the most damning of the four goals, from a United perspective, as Como’s centre-half scores from open play. The ball is worked out to Kaiki, who is afforded the freedom of Lombardy to look up, settle himself, before spinning in a cross which Ramon plants beyond Lammens from close range. Stunning from Como, but there was absolutely zero resistance.

Jacobo Ramón gets another for Como, as they now lead 4-0! 🤯 An unbelievable performance against Manchester United 👏 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SnzpwT7sSV

Tielemans finds Mbeumo between the lines early and the Cameroon forward earns himself a yard of space before unleashing a strike which floats over the bar. Better intent from United, but it is all too little, too late.

The wind has really picked up and is taking control of balls sent skywards. Perhaps sensing this, United, building from a back three, try punching balls through the lines. Mbeumo and Zirkzee combine before playing in Dalot, whose cross flies across the phase of goal without troubling any United forwards.

Another change, this time from Fabregas, as Como’s captain Da Cunha makes way for full-back Kaiki.

Not a good night for the United captain Fernandes, who makes way for Zirkzee. The Portugal midfielder is naturally not best pleased, he trudges down the touchline shaking his head.

A 50/50 lands at the feet of Paz with green grass to run into. He slips in Da Cunha down the right, but his cross is charged down.

United go up the other end and Amad, who has offered something resembling a spark down the right, fires in a shot which Butez does well to tip over. The Como goalkeeper is also quick off his line to deal with the resulting corner.

Fabregas makes a change, Caqueret replacing the tiring Baturina.

Fernandes spots Amad darting in behind, but his flighted cross runs out to Butez.

United are leaving themselves more and more exposed at the back with every foray forward.

Fernandes is the latest United effort to try their luck from distance. His effort balloons high and wide. Who’s next?

Tielemans has a go from the edge of the box, but his tame effort dribbles to Butez.

Como 3 Manchester United 0 (Paz) That is horrific from United. Baleba, brought on to solve problems, only injects more anxiety into this most hapless of away displays with a careless pass around the corner to no one on the far side. Paz collects the ball and darts towards goal, unopposed, and steadies himself before shaping the ball around Lammens.

Nico Paz capitalises on a mistake from Carlos Baleba to extend Como's lead against Manchester United to 3-0 😱 He's been involved in each goal 👏 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/D7kD8PGtcY

Close! Da Cunha almost makes it three, but his curled effort from the right of the box flies just past the outside of the post.

Mount then stumbles on the ball deep inside his half, and Milla is there to snatch it off him. Nothing comes of it, but it is just further evidence of United’s carelessness with the ball.

Well, that just about sums up United this evening. Mount blasts the ball off target from distance to a chorus of boos/jeers. Whether they came from the home or away supporters is unclear.

Como 2 Manchester United 0 (Douvikas) Paz is at it again, this time on the transition, sliding in a wonderful through-ball for Douvikas, who had made a cutting diagonal run, to sweep beyond Lammens. United’s defence caught out once more, just when the visitors looked like they were finally establishing some competitiveness in this match.

Como extend their lead to 2-0 against Manchester United early in the second half! Anastasios Douvikas gets the goal 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/2O9qRG75tG

The surprise is that Carrick waited until half-time to make those much-needed changes.

Paz loses possession in United’s left channel and Dalot pounces on the loose ball, driving towards the by-line before swinging in a cross, which is collected by Butez. Better from United, though.

Baleba’s first involvement is a strong challenge. United will need that type of resolve if they are to get anything from this second half.

Carrick has seen enough and brings on Amad and Baleba in place of Cunha and Santos as United look to overturn Como’s one-goal lead.

Como are controlling things in almost every department...

Possession: Como 64 per cent, Manchester United 36 per centBig chances: Como 1, Manchester United 0Total shots: Como 5, Manchester United 3Expected goals: Como 0.4, Manchester United 0.1

Man Utd become the first time in history to concede in the first two minutes of back-to-back major European matches: 1' vs. Atlético Madrid 2' vs. Como https://t.co/6kJyHmAIni

United enjoy a spell inside the attacking third to close the half, but it’s too late, at least for the first 45 minutes. The referee blows his whistle and we reach half-time with Como a goal to the good.

There are boos at half-time from United’s travelling support.

United send both of their full-backs forward and it gives Cunha the space to get a shot away from just outside of the box, but his curled effort sails over.

There will be one minute of time added on at the end of this half.

That’s a let off for United. Yan Couto, one of two former Manchester City signings in the Como team, carves open the United defence with a lovely pass and Douvikas should have done better with the finish.

Amazing the difference when you have a centre forward prepared to run in behind. Who would have thought it?

Baturina is the latest to threaten Lammens’ goal. His strike from the edge of the box stings the Belgian’s gloves and Douvikas, who attempts to latch on to the rebound, is offside.

Penalty shout for Como! Douvikas is sent through and it looks as though Lammens is in trouble as he sticks out a leg over which the Greek tumbles, but replays show Lammens withdraws his outstretched limb in the nick of time.

There was also an offside in the build-up, so it does not matter anyway.

Milla and Perrone are really pulling the strings in Como’s midfield. The former comes from the Jose Bordalas/Getafe school of football (think Tony Pulis during peak Britannia era) but you would not guess it given the way he manipulates the ball.

This game has entered into something of a holding pattern, with Como retaining possession as United chase shadows, desperately trying to lock off the centre of the park.

Here, Coute inverts, picking up the ball in the inside right channels before spinning in a ball over the top for Douvikas to stride on to, but the Greece forward shanks his shot over the bar.

Thirty four minutes in and the first chants of “attack, attack, attack” can be heard from the United fans. There is currently a giant hole where you would expect United’s strikers to be. It’s so poor.

Lammens does well to get down smartly and keep out a Douvikas effort, speared towards the near post after a sweeping counter attack. The resulting corner fails to threaten United’s defensive unit.

Da Cunha, fresh off his first France call-up, has just sold Mazraoui a dream, spinning the Moroccan in the middle of the pitch before gliding upfield, sweeping the ball out to Valle on the left, whose cross is far too loopy to trouble Lammens.

For seemingly the first time in this match, one of United’s full-backs, Mazraoui, makes a darting run in behind. While the ball goes through to the goalkeeper, it’s the right sort of intent.

Paz escapes the vicious clutches of Santos, but bumps into Cunha’s outstretched leg and earns a foul near the halfway line. Santos, already on a yellow, will need to careful not to get caught doing anything untoward for the remaining 60 minutes of this match.

It’s hard to detect a game plan from United. Como look like they know what what they’ve been told to do but United are just all over the place. Andrey Santos will be grateful referee Sven Jablonski was lenient the first time he came through the back of Paz because he’s just scythed through him a second time minutes later and picked up a yellow.

That’s better from United. Cunha hits the by-line aggressively but his cross is cut out.

Paz then breaks away down the right and, sensing a lack of cover, Santos dives in and receives a yellow card for his troubles.

United string together perhaps their best sequence of the match, shifting the ball quickly from one side to the other, with Mount and Cunha combining, but the move breaks down when Tielemans’ attempted through-ball is cut out by Kempf.

Fernandes attempts to play in Tielemans between the lines but his pass is behind the Belgian and Como regain possession. It’s rinse and repeat moments later, but on the far side.

The detail on United’s passes has been so poor thus far, with Como picking up loose balls all over the pitch.

Penalty shout for Como! Da Cunha, Douvikas and Baturina combine expertly through the middle, trading the ball with cultured one-touch passes. Baturina is felled by Maguire inside United’s box just as he was gearing up to shoot, but neither the referee nor the VAR are minded to intervene. There is a touch, but it does seem very slight.

United have gone with the box midfield once more, with Fernandes rolling inside as a false 9. Como are counteracting United’s movements through Paz dropping in, so Carrick’s men are struggling to take control of the central zones.

Mbeumo bursts towards the by-line but Ramon gets back sharply to divert the ball behind for a corner, which is easily dealt with.

United drop into a deep block, forcing Como to build around the outside. The ball is worked to the adventurous Couto who loses his boot after an overzealous challenge from Cunha and he earns a free-kick for his troubles, but Da Cunha’s delivery fails to beat the first man.

Chance! Da Cunha plays a lovely through-ball into the right channel for Paz to gallop on to and he flashes the ball across the face of goal, but Maguire gets there before Douvikas and the ball is cleared.

United are struggling to string passes together as Paz cuts out a Lammens pass out from the back, but he cannot keep the ball in play.

United need to settle, and here they decide it best to keep hold of the ball for a while. There are a few sideways passes but the ball goes back to Como.

Valle makes a burst down the left and Dalot’s contact results in a foul, but the free-kick is not up to much.

Como 1 Manchester United 0 (Paz) Well, we said he was special! Como work the ball out to the right, with Da Cunha picking out Paz on the edge of the box. Neither of United’s centre-halves are minded to close the Argentine down, and he opens up his body before shaping the ball around Lammens and inside the far post. Golazo.

But the visitors pounce after nicking the ball in Como’s half, Cunha flighting a lovely ball out to Dalot, whose effort sails over the bar.

Fernandes gets us going in Lombardy, with United kicking from right to left.

Como are in their home blue strip while the visitors wear their “third” cream shirts and black shorts.

United are ready, waiting for their opponents in the Sinigaglia tunnel. Da Cunha eventually joins Fernandes at the front of the teams’ respective lines before the players emerge on to the pitch to the Champions League anthem.

Carrick has flitted between five different left-backs in United’s 10 matches this season (Diogo Dalot, Ayden Heaven, Luke Shaw, Noussair Mazraoui and Patrick Dorgu), which underlines why many felt that adding depth to the position in the summer was a priority.

Interest in Newcastle United’s Lewis Hall came to nothing, and there was even a deadline-day enquiry made about Manchester City’s Rayan Aït-Nouri.

Harry Amass has been a feature on United’s bench this season and some thought the 19-year-old could become Carrick’s sixth left-back of the season, but it looks as though Mazraoui will play there tonight.

Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick said before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

“But I have to say, the type of performance put into the weekend and for large parts against Atlético, there’s a lot of togetherness there. There’s a lot of will and determination to do better and wanting to do it for each other, which is important.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of Manchester United’s trip to Como in the Champions League. Under normal circumstances, a visit to the idyllic Lombardy city would be a source of thrill and wonder, but Michael Carrick heads into the eye of a literal and proverbial storm at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia with his team desperately hoping to reverse their fortunes.

Two wins – against Ipswich Town and Sabah – in United’s first 10 matches of the season, a public outburst from Lisandro Martínez and accusations of a “toxic culture” at the club have piled pressure on Carrick. And an uninspiring draw at Elland Road on Sunday did little to settle the rising tide of discontent within the United fanbase.

When asked for his team news, the first words that came from the United head coach’s mouth were: “Right, bit of mixed bag to be honest.” That was not a great sign, and Carrick will be without Martínez, Kobbie Mainoo, Luke Shaw, Ayden Heaven, Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko and Patrick Dorgu, who are injured, while Leny Yoro serves a suspension following his red card against Atlético Madrid.

Like United, the hosts are without a handful of key players, with Moise Kean, Trevoh Chalobah, Assane Diao and Jesus Rodriguez missing from the match-day squad. The abundantly talented Argentine No 10 Nico Paz will feature, however, and he will be keen to showcase his talents in the Champions League.

Como have ascended from Serie B to Europe’s top table in three seasons (and from bankruptcy in nine) under Cesc Fàbregas’ watchful eye. The Spaniard is a minority owner and shareholder of the club, but as head coach he has introduced an incisive, possession-based style of play which contains hints of the managerial greats under whom he played: Arsène Wenger, Pep Guardiola, José Mourinho, Vicente del Bosque, Antonio Conte etc.

#1357. Everton Duo Help England Reach Quarter-Finals

Jordan Pickford edged closer to a century of caps for the England national team on Thursday evening, with James Garner also featuring in a 2-1 victory over Croatia that booked passage to the UEFA Nations League quarter-final stage.

Confirmed by Thomas Tuchel as England’s continuing number one at the start of the international break, Pickford started at Wembley in his 94th senior Three Lions outing.

The spotlight for the evening, however, was firmly on Harry Kane. The Bayern Munich striker was fresh from picking up the Ballon D’Or and made yet more history by surpassing Peter Shilton’s long-held record of 125 England appearances.

Garner and Jarrad Branthwaite, meanwhile, were both on the bench, but only the former would take to the field.

By the time Tuchel made a triple substitution in the 77nd minute – with Garner replacing Arsenal captain Declan Rice in midfield – Kane had already restored England’s lead.

Morgan Rogers had given the hosts the advantage with a close-range finish in the first half, but an error from defender Jarrell Quansah allowed the Croatians to level on the hour mark.

Kane then converted from the spot five minutes later, before it looked to be a dream cameo from Garner as he found the back of the net himself, but a VAR check confirmed an offside in the build-up to deny a first senior international goal for Everton's 2025/26 Player of the Season.

Branthwaite remained an unused substitute in London and will be hoping for game time when England head to Madrid to take on World and European champions Spain in their final game in Group C.

#1356. Youngsters will get their chance, Bruno Fernandes can thrive and touchline energy will be vital: Key lessons for Man United from incoming boss Mauricio Pochettino's 6-0 USA masterclass

Published: 18:47 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 04:35 EST, 15 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino enjoyed a stellar penultimate game in charge of the United States, thrashing Haiti 6-0.

The newly appointed Manchester United manager has just one game left before sinking his teeth into the job at Old Trafford.

He will link up with United on Wednesday, but first must navigate the second leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final tie with Haiti on Tuesday.

Here, Pochettino cut a fairly reserved figure on the touchline as he was rewarded for trusting youth - and even saw his team score from a corner, something United don't do much of these days.

Without further ado, here are four things Manchester United fans learned from the win.

Mauricio Pochettino, dressed in a scarf, was fairly reserved as the United States beat Haiti 6-0

Pochettino’s arrival spells good news for United’s proud tradition of promoting homegrown youth - it is glad tidings for the likes of Shea Lacey and Kobbie Mainoo. You wonder if, for a while, JJ Gabriel will look on forlornly from Real Madrid’s reserves.

The Argentinian handed out 13 debuts in the September-October international break, including to eight teenagers in one 4-1 victory over Peru.

His strategy was no different here as he started 18-year-old Julian Hall up front and Diego Kochen, 20, in goal - both players he has given debuts to this year. He was rewarded, with Hall scoring his fourth goal in just five games for the United States, while Kochen kept a clean sheet.

Despite his affinity for the stars of tomorrow, he is a hard schoolmaster. In a column for The Athletic in 2022, he revealed that he sat a young Harry Kane down for a brutal meeting where he showed him stats and clips to justify why he wasn’t playing him more.

Pochettino had known Kane’s potential from their first training session but wanted the ‘tough conversation’ to get the best out of him. Kane went on to score 169 goals under him for Tottenham, and now he’s the best player in the world.

His trust in fresh faces could inject some much-needed enthusiasm around the club, strengthen the squad's connection with the fanbase, and increase the energy levels in one of the Premier League's oldest, most lethargic teams.

The likes of Shea Lacey will be delighted at how Pochettino puts trust in younger players

Julian Hall, 18, struck his fourth goal in five games for the United States under Pochettino

Pochettino has a history of getting the most out of attacking midfielders such as Dele Alli, Christian Eriksen, and Adam Lallana. You can add Cole Palmer to that list too, though he was primarily a right winger under him at Chelsea.

Manchester United desperately need him to get a tune out of Bruno Fernandes, who has cut a frustrated figure this season and whose creative efficiency has declined - though he still has nine goal involvements.

If Christian Pulisic’s performance against Haiti is anything to go by, Fernandes will be happy. The attacking midfielder scored twice, playing a free role and being given penalty duty.

The 28-year-old was also asked to muck in defensively, and that’s something Fernandes is willing to do. Across the seasons, he has often covered more ground than any of his team-mates.

Pochettino and Pulisic have seemingly had a distant relationship, despite the latter’s insistence to the contrary. The manager branded it ‘b*******’ when the AC Milan star opted out of the Gold Cup last year, and left him out of his selection a couple of months ago, bringing in 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan.

Asked about Pochettino's upcoming final game, Pulisic said at full-time: 'We're treating it like any other game.' No emotion on display.

Depending on how you interpret Fernandes - either a die-for-the-badge club servant or a primadonna - Pochettino could draw the best or worst out of the Portuguese.

Pochettino often gets the best out of attacking midfielders - will he work well with Bruno Fernandes?

He has had a distant relationship with Christian Pulisic, but the AC Milan star scored twice here

Pochettino tends to push his defensive lines high up the pitch and his strategy with the United States has been no different.

They were almost caught out for trying to play the offside trap early on as a simple ball from midfield sent Danley Jean Jacques through one-on-one, forcing Kochen into a good save.

Meanwhile, full-backs Antonee Robinson and Alex Freeman were constantly pushing high and overlapping in his 4-2-3-1 system - although you’d obviously expect a strong level of intent when they’re favourites against Haiti.

Given his high-line tradition, Pochettino may well favour more mobile defenders such as Leny Yoro and Patrick Dorgu.

The battle for Harry Maguire will be to convince his new boss that his other qualities compensate for his lack of pace.

Pochettino takes inspiration from the frenetic football of Marcelo Bielsa, who managed him at Newell’s Old Boys in Argentina.

But he'll have to balance his philosophy with the reality of United's woeful defensive record this campaign. Just the 15 goals conceded in the last five games...

Pochettino showed an eagerness to intervene early in the game - a possible boost after Michael Carrick suffered from slow starts

Pochettino is typically seen as an animated character on the touchline, in contrast to Carrick's statesmanlike behaviour, but he spent lots of time in his seat here.

He has calmed down somewhat these days - though he did kick a crate of bottles in frustration at the World Cup - and didn’t even react much when his team scored.

A major criticism of Carrick is that he takes too long to change things in-game, often going late with substitutions. Pochettino has traditionally leaned that way, too, but he was eager to influence proceedings here.

Even three minutes in, at a break while Antonee Robinson was being treated, he called Pulisic over for what looked like an intense tactical chat.

United have been plagued by slow starts this season, so it was encouraging to see Pochettino so alert and full of ideas early into the game. He could have coasted, really, but wanted to eke out every advantage.

#1355. Severe drought and warming increase the extinction risk of cacti

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Extreme climatic events are increasing in frequency and intensity with climate change1. Their effects on species’ distributions and extinction risk remain poorly understood2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Most species distribution models rely on long-term mean climate, overlooking potentially important nonlinear effects of extremes. Here we integrate new spatial data on severe drought10, including compounding effects of warmer temperatures, with a comprehensive curated dataset of cactus occurrences (648,316 records) and species distribution models to assess how severe drought alters projected suitable climatic area for 993 species of Cactaceae, a highly threatened family11 that is commonly considered drought tolerant. In 91% of cases, models including severe drought were better supported than mean-climate models. Across emissions scenarios (Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) SSP1-2.6 to SSP5-8.5) with 100-km dispersal, including severe drought increased the share of species losing suitable climatic area from 58–61% to 69–72%. The proportion of species projected to lose over a quarter of suitable area increased from 26–43% to 55–58%, and the proportion projected to lose over four-fifths increased from 1–15% to 25–35%. With severe drought, restricting dispersal from 100 to 0 km increased the share losing suitable area from 69–72% to 84–85% across SSPs. These declines reduced regional richness, with five bioregions potentially losing over 25% of species. These findings demonstrate that accounting for climatic extremes can alter assessments of biodiversity vulnerability under climate change. Integrating climatic extremes into ecological forecasting will be critical for assessing biodiversity loss and designing effective conservation strategies across taxa and ecosystems.

Given the data sharing agreement with iNaturalist and private contributors and the widespread risk of illegal collection in Cactaceae, occurrence data used for analyses are available only on request. Requests should be made through correspondence with the corresponding author and, depending on the taxonomic scope of the request, may require an agreement with one or more of the authors (data derived from BIEN or private contributors) or with iNaturalist directly, prohibiting further data sharing. Requests should include a complete list of data users and their affiliations, the purpose of the request, the taxonomic scope and a disclosure of any competing interests. Partially obscured iNaturalist data are available72. Average climatic data were retrieved from the CHELSA repository, version 2.1 (https://chelsa-climate.org/). SPEI drought data are available from the NASA Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC; https://www.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/globaldrought/). Soil layers were downloaded from the SoilGrids repository, version 2.0 (https://www.isric.org/explore/soilgrids). Expert distribution maps used to create Extended Data Fig. 7 were obtained from the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species and the IUCN SSC Cactus and Succulent Plants Specialist Group. Bioregion data were downloaded from a previous study52. All Figures and Extended Data Figures are directly reproducible from the Supplementary Information and code at Zenodo123.

All code is available at GitHub (https://github.com/mdpillet/DroughtForecasts) and archived at Zenodo123.

Each panel shows the probability density of predicted changes in suitable climatic area relative to the present for a particular dispersal distance and SSP. The vertical dashed line indicates no predicted change in suitable climatic area. Green shading indicates an increase in suitable area, whereas red shading indicates a decrease in area. The x axis uses a square-root transformation to facilitate visualization. For comparison to other figures, only densities up to 12 are shown on the y-axis. No spatial thinning of occurrences was performed. Predictions were not clamped, allowing for extrapolation beyond the observed range of variables for the present during model fitting. The maximum true skill statistic (sensitivity plus specificity minus one) was used as the threshold to transform continuous suitability predictions to binary presence/absence predictions.

Each panel shows the probability density of predicted changes in suitable climatic area relative to the present for a particular dispersal distance and SSP. The vertical dashed line indicates no predicted change in suitable climatic area. Green shading indicates an increase in suitable area, whereas red shading indicates a decrease in area. The x axis uses a square-root transformation to facilitate visualization. For comparison to other figures, only densities up to 12 are shown on the y axis. Occurrences were thinned at a distance of 5 km. Predictions were clamped to reduce extrapolation by limiting features to one standard deviation beyond the range observed for the present during model fitting. The maximum true skill statistic (sensitivity plus specificity minus one) was used as the threshold to transform continuous suitability predictions to binary presence/absence predictions.

Each panel shows the probability density of predicted changes in suitable climatic area relative to the present for a particular dispersal distance and SSP. The vertical dashed line indicates no predicted change in suitable climatic area. Green shading indicates an increase in suitable area, whereas red shading indicates a decrease in area. The x axis uses a square-root transformation to facilitate visualization. For comparison to other figures, only densities up to 12 are shown on the y axis. Occurrences were thinned at a distance of 10 km. Predictions were clamped to reduce extrapolation by limiting features to one standard deviation beyond the range observed for the present during model fitting. The maximum true skill statistic (sensitivity plus specificity minus one) was used as the threshold to transform continuous suitability predictions to binary presence/absence predictions.

Each panel shows the probability density of predicted changes in suitable climatic area relative to the present for a particular dispersal distance and SSP. The vertical dashed line indicates no predicted change in suitable climatic area. Green shading indicates an increase in suitable area, whereas red shading indicates a decrease in area. The x axis uses a square-root transformation to facilitate visualization. For comparison to other figures, only densities up to 12 are shown on the y axis. No spatial thinning of occurrences was performed. Only predictions based on models with a ratio of the number of presences to the number of model coefficients greater than 10 are shown. Predictions were clamped to reduce extrapolation by limiting features to one standard deviation beyond the range observed for the present during model fitting. The maximum true skill statistic (sensitivity plus specificity minus one) was used as the threshold to transform continuous suitability predictions to binary presence/absence predictions.

Each panel shows the probability density of predicted changes in suitable climatic area relative to the present for a particular dispersal distance and SSP. The vertical dashed line indicates no predicted change in suitable climatic area. Green shading indicates an increase in suitable area, whereas red shading indicates a decrease in area. The x axis uses a square-root transformation to facilitate visualization. For comparison to other figures, only densities up to 12 are shown on the y axis. No spatial thinning of occurrences was performed. Predictions were clamped to reduce extrapolation by limiting features to one standard deviation beyond the range observed for the present during model fitting. Equal sensitivity and specificity was used as the threshold to transform continuous suitability predictions to binary presence/absence predictions.

Each panel shows the probability density of predicted changes in suitable climatic area relative to the present for a particular dispersal distance and SSP. The vertical dashed line indicates no predicted change in suitable climatic area. Green shading indicates an increase in suitable area, whereas red shading indicates a decrease in area. The x axis uses a square-root transformation to facilitate visualization. For comparison to other figures, only densities up to 12 are shown on the y axis. No spatial thinning of occurrences was performed. Predictions were clamped to reduce extrapolation by limiting features to one standard deviation beyond the range observed for the present during model fitting. The omission rate was controlled at the 10th percentile as the threshold to transform continuous suitability predictions to binary presence/absence predictions.

Niche overlap is expressed using Schoener’s D (left) and the I similarity statistic (right). Values are binned using a bin width of 0.025. n = 2,048.

Maps of current and future predicted richness for different SSPs, with/without clamping, different dispersal distances and different thresholds. Only maps without spatial thinning of occurrence data are included.

Model statistics for final models (1,014 species) by variable set, GCM and spatial thinning distance. The column ‘Lambda rule’ refers to the method for choosing the regularization parameter λ (Methods).

Variables included for final models, after filtering models with AUC below or equal to 0.7 and/or a Boyce index below or equal to 0.5 (8,892 models for 993 species), by variable set, GCM and spatial thinning distance.

Changes in predicted suitable climatic area (700,488 predictions for 993 taxa) by taxon, spatial thinning distance, model type, GCM, SSP, clamping options, dispersal distance and threshold type.

Model quality (AUC and Boyce index) for a subset of a hundred randomly selected species (99 after removal of L. quadricostatus, for which sample size requirements were not met) by environmental outlier filtering approach, spatial thinning distance, background size, variable set and GCM.

Number of occurrences by species (n = 1,189), along with the number of occurrences removed with and without filtering of environmental outliers.

Taxonomic review of occurrence data, based on the TNRS R package.

Review of native status of occurrence data, based on the NSR R package.

#1353. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

Emery had warned his players of complacency against the Norwegian champions, but Villa took command from the start and were ahead after 23 minutes.

Ross Barkley scored twice against Fenerbahce last week and was in the right place again to head Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner past Arild Ostbo.

They had led 2-0 at half-time before rescuing a point in the last minute.

Hopes of another famous European night here never appeared likely, even though their 2,500 travelling supporters remained noisy all evening.

Villa were awarded a second goal after Alysson was brought down in the penalty area by Zlatko Tripic.

Speaking to the club’s official website in his match preview, the Aston Villa boss said: “Champions League, every team they are playing Champions League, they are because they deserve it and they are dangerous and they have their collective and individual issues or characteristics as a team.

“Viking, they drew against Bayern Munich last week, they lost against Stuttgart. They are with Bodø/Glimt in the league, first and second with the same points.

“Bodø/Glimt is a team successful the last years in Europe, performing well, getting good results, playing Champions League, beating important teams.

“So Viking now is a new team as well, with the with the capacity to draw against Bayern Munich, the capacity as well to compete against Stuttgart and to compete against us tomorrow.

“This is Champions League, and Champions League is very difficult. In Champions League, we have now six points, it’s something amazing, but very difficult, and to keep the same way we are is our challenge.

“It’s not only Champions League, because Europa League is very difficult, and Conference League is very difficult. Europe is always very difficult.

“This is the first respect. We are Champions League, and each team is, of course, very, very respectful for us.”

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, Villa were stepping into the unknown despite the arrival of ten new players.

We have all learned, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their Champions League campaign so far and are running into fine form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Champions League fixture as Aston Villa host Viking in the Midlands.

Villa made history in their previous home Champions League outing last week, thrashing Fenerbahce 6-0 to seal the club’s biggest-ever European win. This emphatic victory, coupled with the hard-fought 3-2 triumph over Club Brugge at the start of September, means that Unai Emery’s side have made a 100% winning start to the league phase. The well-deserved 1-0 Premier League victory over Newcastle United at St James’ Park on Saturday evening has amplified the positivity, with Emery’s new-look squad beginning to meaningfully gel and now boast a five-match unbeaten streak across all competitions.

Prepared for another night on Europe's biggest stage ✨ https://t.co/oZYiIiGvRg

Despite their Viking’s lack of European pedigree, Villa should be wary of their Norwegian opponents, who secured an unforgettable 3-3 draw with Bayern Munich in Stavanger last time out in the Champions League. The hosts initially flew into a two-goal lead at the break, before a double from Harry Kane and a strike from Luiz Diaz hauled the Bavarians ahead. However, after Michael Olise was sent off, Herman Haugen’s 90th-minute headed equaliser rescued a thrilling draw to give Viking their European point this season following a 3-1 loss to Stuttgart on MD1. Domestically, the reigning champions of Norway are joint top of the Eliteserien with Bodo/Glimt and embroiled in a nailbiting title race with just seven games remaining.

Villa’s injury list includes Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Johan Manzambi, who both picked up issues against Newcastle, as well as Amadou Onana and Matteo Ruggeri. Still, the hosts possess more than enough quality to dismantle Viking, particularly with Nicolas Jackson, who has been in effective form recently and netted a brilliant brace against Fenerbahce.

We’ll bring you the latest updates and drama. Kick-off is at 20:00, with team news coming shortly.
